extracted.intended_audience: Citizens, legislators, and readers concerned with constitutional design (originally the people of New York and those debating the proposed federal Constitution).
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing principles for structuring government power among legislative, executive, and judicial departments, with attention to necessary separations, permitted mixtures, and practical checks to prevent usurpation. The text evaluates historical examples and state constitutions to derive design criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of accumulation of whole powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The accumulation of all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, in the same hands—whether of one, a few, or many—may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: A constitution must avoid vesting the whole power of one department in the same person or body that possesses the whole power of another. If one entity exercises the entire legislative power and the entire executive or judicial power, liberty is subverted. (Textual support: “The accumulation of all powers ... may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny.”)

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct meaning of 'separate and distinct' departments
rubrics_metrics.description: The maxim that departments ought to be separate and distinct does not require absolute isolation; it forbids that the WHOLE power of one department be exercised by the same hands which possess the WHOLE power of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Interpret Montesquieu as barring total fusion of departmental powers, not any partial agency. Example: in the British constitution the executive has some legislative-adjacent powers (treaty-making with force of law under limits) and appoints judges, yet the whole powers are not united. The design test is whether entire powers of one are in the hands of another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial mixture/agency between departments is permissible and sometimes necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Departments may have partial agency in or control over the acts of each other—some blending is consistent with free government and often unavoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from state constitutions: executive qualified negative (veto) on legislation; Senate as tribunal for impeachment; judges appointed by executive; legislative appointment of some officers. New Hampshire’s qualification: keep departments separate 'as the nature of a free government will admit.' Use these partial links to provide mutual control rather than to consolidate whole power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide constitutional controls so departments can check one another
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless the departments are so connected and blended as to give each a constitutional control over the others, the separation required for liberty cannot be maintained in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design principle: embed reciprocal constitutional mechanisms (e.g., veto, impeachment, appointment/removal procedures, judicial review mechanisms) that enable each branch to contest encroachments by others. The absence of such practical controls will render paper boundaries ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative encroachment is the principal practical danger
rubrics_metrics.description: In representative republics the legislative department, by its extent, facility of masking encroachments, access to public resources, and influence over rewards of office, is the most likely to extend its power and threaten liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning and evidence: legislature can draw all power into its 'impetuous vortex,' mask encroachments under complicated measures, control public money and salaries, and thereby create dependence. Historical examples (Virginia, Pennsylvania) show legislatures assuming judicial and executive functions. Design should pay special heed to restraining legislative overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parchment barriers alone are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely marking departmental boundaries in a constitution (parchment barriers) is not an adequate security against encroaching power; practical safeguards are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: experience from state governments shows constitutional text without enforcement or countervailing controls failed to prevent usurpations. Jefferson’s observation: 'BUT NO BARRIER WAS PROVIDED BETWEEN THESE SEVERAL POWERS.' Use institutional checks, not just declaratory clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dependence of executive and judiciary on legislature for subsistence
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaving the judiciary and executive dependent on the legislature for subsistence in office (appointments, tenure, salaries) undermines their independence and their capacity to check legislative encroachments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: judges’ salaries varied by legislature; appointments and removals controlled by legislative majorities. Design implication: create appointment/tenure and salary protections (or distributed appointment/removal powers) to reduce capture by the legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against 'elective despotism' by dividing and balancing powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Even elective bodies can become despotic if powers are concentrated; the remedy is to divide and balance powers among several bodies so no one can transcend legal limits without being checked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson’s warning: 'An ELECTIVE DESPOTISM was not the government we fought for.' Use multiple independent bodies, mutual checks, and balanced appointments to prevent an elective majority from exercising despotic authority (example: Venice as a negative example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and avoid legislative usurpation anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific abuses by legislatures indicate usurpation: passing laws without required prior publication/printing, varying constitutionally fixed judge salaries, drawing judicial cases into legislative determination, and assuming executive powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical checklist/anti-patterns from Pennsylvania and Council of Censors reports: look for laws that circumvent procedural safeguards (e.g., no prior printing), encroach on jury trial, unconstitutionally modify judicial compensation or jurisdiction, or take on executive functions. Such signs point to constitutional breaches requiring corrective design or enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical/state examples to inform practical protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine how existing state constitutions mixed powers (e.g., New Hampshire, Massachusetts, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia) to understand workable combinations of partial agency and controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: draw lessons from concrete provisions—qualified negatives (vetoes), impeachment by one branch and trial by another, executive appointment with legislative confirmation or council, ex‑officio roles—assessing which mixtures produce effective checks and which produce dangerous consolidations. The text catalogues many variants as a design resource.
